title: Explain AQE's three major optimizations: (1) post-shuffle partition coalescing (combines many small partitions into fewer larger ones), (2) skew join optimization (detects and splits oversized partitions), (3) dynamic join strategy change (e.g., converting a shuffle join to a broadcast join based on actual data size).

s1_definition.profdef: Adaptive Query Execution delivers three major runtime optimizations. Post-shuffle partition coalescing merges many small shuffle partitions into fewer, larger partitions so the next stage has fewer and better-sized tasks. Skew join optimization detects shuffle partitions that are abnormally large and splits them into smaller sub-partitions, replicating the matching side, so a single hot key no longer produces one long-running straggler task. Dynamic join strategy change replaces a planned shuffle join, such as sort-merge, with a broadcast join when AQE discovers at runtime that one side is small enough to broadcast.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture clerks at the National Bank of India dividing up branch files after a big re-sort. First, coalescing is when the supervisor sees many clerks each holding a nearly empty folder and combines them so fewer clerks carry fuller, balanced folders — no wasted desks. Second, skew handling is when one clerk is buried under a mountain of files for one huge branch while others sit idle, so the supervisor splits that mountain across several clerks. Third, dynamic join change is when two teams were going to do a slow full re-sort to combine their lists, but the supervisor notices one team's list is tiny and simply photocopies it to everyone, skipping the re-sort entirely.
s1_definition.oneliner: AQE coalesces tiny partitions into balanced ones, splits oversized skewed partitions to kill stragglers, and switches a shuffle join to a broadcast join when a side turns out small.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Adaptive Query Execution delivers three major runtime optimizations. Post-shuffle partition coalescing merges many small shuffle partitions into fewer, larger partitions so the next stage has fewer and better-sized tasks. Skew join optimization detects shuffle partitions that are abnormally large and splits them into smaller sub-partitions, replicating the matching side, so a single hot key no longer produces one long-running straggler task. Dynamic join strategy change replaces a planned shuffle join, such as sort-merge, with a broadcast join when AQE discovers at runtime that one side is small enough to broadcast.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture clerks at the National Bank of India dividing up branch files after a big re-sort. First, coalescing is when the supervisor sees many clerks each holding a nearly empty folder and combines them so fewer clerks carry fuller, balanced folders — no wasted desks. Second, skew handling is when one clerk is buried under a mountain of files for one huge branch while others sit idle, so the supervisor splits that mountain across several clerks. Third, dynamic join change is when two teams were going to do a slow full re-sort to combine their lists, but the supervisor notices one team's list is tiny and simply photocopies it to everyone, skipping the re-sort entirely.

**One line to remember:** AQE coalesces tiny partitions into balanced ones, splits oversized skewed partitions to kill stragglers, and switches a shuffle join to a broadcast join when a side turns out small.

sections.s2_technical:
The first optimization is post-shuffle partition coalescing. By default a shuffle produces a fixed large number of partitions, often two hundred, regardless of how much data there actually is. After a filter or aggregation, many of those partitions can end up nearly empty, which means the next stage launches hundreds of tiny tasks, each with scheduling overhead that dwarfs its tiny workload. AQE reads the real post-shuffle partition sizes and merges adjacent small partitions into fewer partitions that are each close to a target size, so the next stage runs a sensible number of appropriately sized tasks. This is controlled by the coalesce-partitions setting and an advisory target partition size.

The second optimization is skew join handling. Data skew happens when one key has vastly more records than others, so after the shuffle one partition is enormous while the rest are small. In a join, the task handling that giant partition becomes a straggler that runs long after every other task finishes, and it can even run out of memory. AQE detects a partition as skewed when it exceeds both a factor of the median partition size and an absolute byte threshold, then splits that oversized partition into several smaller sub-partitions and replicates the matching rows from the other side of the join so each sub-partition can be joined independently. The result is that the hot key's work is spread across many tasks instead of crushing one.

The third optimization is dynamic join strategy change. Before the job runs, Catalyst must choose a join algorithm from size estimates, and if it thinks both sides are large it picks a shuffle join like sort-merge. But after an upstream filter or aggregation, one side may actually be tiny. At the shuffle boundary AQE sees the real size, and if one side now fits under the broadcast threshold it converts the shuffle join into a broadcast hash join, shipping the small side to every executor and skipping the expensive shuffle of the large side entirely.

A senior nuance is that these three work together and all key off the same runtime statistics gathered at shuffle boundaries, and all are on by default in modern Spark. Coalescing is almost always a free win; skew handling removes the most common cause of mysterious straggler tasks; and dynamic join switching captures the frequent case where filtering shrinks a table below the broadcast limit. Still, AQE is not magic — extreme skew sometimes needs manual salting, the broadcast threshold must be set sensibly for executor memory, and none of this helps a job with no shuffle. In the bank, these three together turned several fragile, skew-prone nightly joins into stable, fast jobs without rewriting the queries.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — After filtering, the shuffle left hundreds of nearly empty partitions, wasting tasks. This is exactly what coalescing fixes.

Problem 2 — One huge branch's data created a single straggler task in a join. This is exactly what skew splitting fixes.

Problem 3 — A dimension table turned out tiny after filtering, but the plan still did a slow shuffle join. This is exactly what dynamic join switching fixes.

The mini-project models the three optimizations in Java as separate rules operating on runtime partition statistics. `CoalesceRule` merges small partitions toward a target size, `SkewRule` splits oversized partitions, and `JoinSwitchRule` flips a shuffle join to broadcast under the threshold. The demo feeds realistic per-branch partition sizes for accounts of Rajesh and Priya and prints how each rule rewrote the plan.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: five post-shuffle partitions — four branches around ten to twelve megabytes each and one skewed branch, HYD, at four hundred megabytes. The coalesce target is sixty-four megabytes, skew detection needs more than five times the median and more than two hundred fifty-six megabytes, and the broadcast limit is ten megabytes.

Step 1: Coalescing runs first. It walks the partitions accumulating sizes, and because the four small branches together are only around forty-two megabytes, they merge toward the sixty-four-megabyte target, while the four-hundred-megabyte HYD stays on its own. The partition count drops from five to fewer, better-sized partitions.

Step 2: Skew handling runs next on the coalesced partitions. It computes the median size and checks each partition. HYD at four hundred megabytes is far more than five times the median and well over the two-hundred-fifty-six-megabyte threshold, so it is flagged as skewed.

Step 3: The skew rule splits HYD into sub-partitions sized near the threshold, so instead of one giant task there are several balanced sub-tasks, each joinable independently against replicated matching rows.

Step 4: The partition set now has the merged small group plus HYD's sub-partitions, which removes the straggler that would otherwise dominate the stage.

Step 5: Dynamic join switching runs independently on the join. The dimension table is eight megabytes after filtering, under the ten-megabyte broadcast limit, so the planned sort-merge join is converted to a broadcast join and the large side's shuffle is avoided.

Step 6: The final state shows all three optimizations applied — balanced coalesced partitions, split skew, and a broadcast join — producing a plan that is both faster and free of stragglers, none of which the static plan could have achieved.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] AQE coalesce: 5 partitions => 2
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [WARNING] AQE skew: 'HYD' (400000000B) split into 2 sub-partitions
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] partitions after coalesce+skew = 3
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] AQE join switch: side 8000000B <= limit => SORT_MERGE to BROADCAST (shuffle avoided)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] final join strategy = BROADCAST
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Post-shuffle partitions: MUM10 DEL12 BLR9 CHE11 HYD400 (MB)
    │
    ▼ (1) COALESCE toward 64MB
  [MUM+DEL+BLR+CHE ≈ 42MB]   [HYD 400MB]
    │
    ▼ (2) SKEW split (HYD > 5×median AND > 256MB)
  [MUM+DEL+BLR+CHE]   [HYD#sub0 200MB]  [HYD#sub1 200MB]
    │  (one straggler → several balanced sub-tasks)
    ▼ (3) JOIN SWITCH (dimension 8MB <= 10MB broadcast limit)
  SORT_MERGE (shuffle both sides)  ──→  BROADCAST (ship small side, no big shuffle)
    │
    ▼
  Balanced, straggler-free, shuffle-light plan
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Adaptive Query Execution delivers three major optimizations, all driven by real statistics collected at shuffle boundaries. The first is post-shuffle partition coalescing. A shuffle produces a fixed large number of partitions by default, often two hundred, so after a filter or aggregation many of them end up nearly empty, and the next stage wastes effort launching hundreds of tiny tasks whose scheduling overhead dwarfs their work. AQE reads the actual partition sizes and merges adjacent small ones toward a target size, so the next stage runs a sensible number of balanced tasks.

The second is skew join optimization. When one key has far more records than others, one shuffle partition becomes enormous while the rest are small, and the task handling it becomes a straggler that runs long after everything else and can run out of memory. AQE detects a partition as skewed when it exceeds both a factor of the median and an absolute byte threshold, then splits it into smaller sub-partitions and replicates the matching side of the join so each sub-partition joins independently, spreading the hot key's work across many tasks. The third is dynamic join strategy change: Catalyst must pick a join algorithm from estimates before the job runs, but after an upstream filter one side may actually be tiny, so at the shuffle boundary AQE sees the real size and converts a planned sort-merge shuffle join into a broadcast join, shipping the small side everywhere and avoiding the large side's shuffle entirely.

In my project at the National Bank of India these three together turned several fragile, skew-prone nightly joins into stable, fast jobs without my rewriting a single query. Coalescing was essentially a free win on every aggregation, skew splitting eliminated the mysterious straggler tasks we used to see on month-end spikes in one branch, and dynamic join switching repeatedly caught the common case where filtering shrank a dimension table below the broadcast limit. The caution I always add is that AQE is not magic: extreme skew sometimes still needs manual salting, the broadcast threshold must be set sensibly for executor memory, and none of these help a job that has no shuffle in the first place.
